title: Pillar inscription from the reign of Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI read at Kothakota, Telangana
dek: A heritage research group says a three-sided Kannada inscription on a temple pillar in Wanaparthy district records land gifts made in the early 12th century, under the Kalyana Chalukya ruler Vikramaditya VI.
body: Members of the Kotha Telangana Charitra Brundam, a Telangana heritage research group, have documented an inscribed pillar standing in the courtyard of a temple at Kothakota in Wanaparthy district. Telangana Today and Deccan Chronicle reported the find on 9 November 2026, and both say the text had not been read before. The two papers name the temple differently: Telangana Today calls it a Shiva temple, Deccan Chronicle the Kota Anjaneya temple.

Sriramoju Haragopal, the group's president, deciphered the text. According to Telangana Today, the language is Kannada, written in the transitional Telugu-Kannada script of the 12th century. The title Tribhuvanamalla Deva in the text places it in the reign of Vikramaditya VI of the Kalyana (Kalyani) Chalukya dynasty. Deccan Chronicle reports that it is dated in the king's 43rd regnal year; Telangana Today gives the date as 22 May 1118 CE.

The inscription is cut on three faces of the pillar. According to the reports, the first face records that a donor named Kalabolaviranolaba Malladesaraddi washed the feet of Kadiraja, an ascetic or priest, and gave him three mattars of wetland; Deccan Chronicle adds a second donor, Pallayanayaka, who gave 11 mattars. Deccan Chronicle says the gifts were for food offerings at a Keshava temple.

The second face is badly worn, but the name Rameshwara Pandita and a mention of a solar eclipse can still be made out. The third face records a further land grant by a chieftain named Sri Nayaka. The pillar itself is broken diagonally across the middle.

The reading so far comes from the research group, as reported in the press. The reports do not say whether the state archaeology department or the Archaeological Survey of India has examined the pillar, and neither includes a full transcript of the text.
